# Leveraging antibiotic hormesis for cryptic natural product discovery

**Authors:** Joon Soo An; Ellysia N Overton; Mohammad R Seyedsayamdost

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Chemistry, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544 | bDepartment of Molecular Biology, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544

## Abstract

Microbial natural products are a foundational source of therapeutic agents, yet a vast majority remain inaccessible due to the limited expression of their biosynthetic gene clusters under standard laboratory conditions. To address this challenge, we developed a simple and broadly applicable screening approach based on the idea of antibiotic hormesis wherein high-dose growth-inhibitory antibiotics serve as low-dose elicitors of secondary metabolites. We generated an in-house library of all available clinical antibiotics and exposed nine phylogenetically diverse bacteria to high-dose growth inhibition and low-dose metabolite stimulation assays. The approach revealed the induction of cryptic metabolites with every strain tested. Four of these were selected for scale-up fermentation and comprehensive metabolomic analysis, leading to the identification of eight known but strain-novel cryptic metabolites and nine structurally unique, previously undescribed natural products. These findings underscore the utility of the antibiotic hormesis approach as a rapid and scalable platform for the discovery of natural products and therapeutic leads. Moreover, the consistent elicitation of cryptic metabolites highlights the generalizability of low-dose antibiotics as key signaling molecules in microbial metabolic regulation. Beyond expanding the repertoire of accessible natural products, this work lays the foundation for systematic studies into the molecular and ecological mechanisms that govern cryptic metabolite biosynthesis.

Keywords: natural products, cryptic metabolites, low-dose antibiotics, bacteria

Natural products have been a cornerstone of therapeutic discovery (1). Over the past century, compounds such as penicillin, lovastatin, and semaglutide have revolutionized the treatment of infectious diseases, cardiovascular disorders, and metabolic syndromes, respectively. These and other natural product remedies, especially antibiotics and anticancer agents, exemplify the profound therapeutic potential embedded in microbial genomes. However, despite decades of intensive natural product research, recent genome sequencing efforts show that we have only scratched the surface of microbial chemical diversity. The majority of natural product biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) are sparingly expressed or transcriptionally silent, also referred to as cryptic, under standard laboratory growth conditions (2–4). As a result, their products have gone undetected in conventional drug discovery campaigns. New methodologies are needed to access and leverage this hidden repertoire of structurally and functionally diverse natural products (5–11).

Several strategies have recently emerged with the goal of stimulating the production of cryptic metabolites. Among these, we have contributed high-throughput elicitor screening (HiTES), a forward chemical genetics approach that systematically screens small molecules for their ability to induce the expression of silent BGCs (7). HiTES has broad applicability as it avoids elaborate cloning or genetic manipulation procedures and directly links chemical elicitors to metabolic outputs. A striking and recurrent finding from HiTES has been the identification of low-dose antibiotics as the most effective inducers of silent BGCs (7, 12–17). Across diverse microbial taxa, including soil-dwelling actinomycetes, marine bacteria, human microbiome strains, (18) and fungi, (19) subinhibitory concentrations of antibiotics have repeatedly been identified as inducers of silent BGCs, leading to the production of otherwise undetected metabolites. The underlying mechanism of this antibiotic hormesis effect has been investigated in a few cases, revealing that low-dose antibiotics act on their canonical cellular targets, similar to their high-dose, lethal counterparts. However, rather than triggering cell death, these sublethal perturbations activate stress response pathways that include the induction of otherwise dormant secondary metabolite BGCs, in some cases, via canonical transcriptional regulators (17, 20–24).

These observations have led us to formulate a simple yet powerful hypothesis that forms the motivation for the current work: We pose that antibiotics, which inhibit growth at high doses, can broadly act as inducers of cryptic metabolism at low doses. If true, this would offer an exceptionally straightforward approach to cryptic metabolite discovery, one that requires no cloning, genetic engineering, nor elaborate chemical screens. Instead, it would rely on standard antibiotic assays to first identify “high-dose killers,” followed by testing those same antibiotics at subinhibitory concentrations in conjunction with HPLC-MS-based metabolomics to identify “low-dose elicitors” of cryptic metabolites (Fig. 1). This approach would leverage antibiotic hormesis in the search for novel natural products and obviate the need for high-throughput screens, instead relying on simple phenotypic screens and subsequent metabolic profiling with a small number of antibiotics.

*Fig. 1.: Workflow for antibiotic hormesis-based elicitation of cryptic BGCs. A strain is screened against an antibiotic library to find high-dose growth inhibitors. These are then tested as low-dose elicitors of natural products using a readout, such as HPLC–MS. New compounds are then isolated and characterized. Abx, antibiotic; Elc, elicitor; NP, natural product.*

In this study, we systematically test the antibiotic hormesis idea across nine well-studied phylogenetically and ecologically diverse bacterial strains. Our results revealed cryptic metabolites in every single screen. Not every high-dose growth-inhibitor served as a low-dose inducer of secondary metabolism, but we find that >40% of antibiotics exhibit this phenotype among the strains tested, resulting in clear metabolomic shifts. We scaled up cultures of four representative strains under eliciting conditions, performed metabolomic profiling and compound isolation, and identified a eight new-to-strain natural products as well as nine novel cryptic metabolites, including a structurally distinct class that we term beddingiolide. These findings reinforce the emerging view that antibiotics do not merely function as antimicrobial agents at high doses but also as potent modulators of microbial gene expression and secondary metabolism at low doses. They further demonstrate that the antibiotic hormesis strategy is not only conceptually sound but also highly effective in practice, offering a rapid and simple approach for natural product discovery. Antibiotic hormesis thus provides a new approach for accessing the hidden biosynthetic potential of microbes as well as enriching the chemical and functional space of secondary metabolites and possible drug leads.

## Results

Creation of an in-house antibiotic library and hormesis screens. To assess the antibiotics hormesis idea, we first created a custom library of clinical antibiotics. While our prior libraries contained a small number of antibiotics, which were often identified as elicitors, we designed the current library to consist exclusively of antibiotics. Approximately 180 antibiotics have been approved by the FDA. Of these, we were able to procure 133, which were dissolved in DMSO or water at a stock concentration of 1 mM (SI Appendix, Table S1), with the goal of screening these at high doses (~20 μM); those that inhibit growth would then be tested at low doses (1 to 5 μM) using UPLC-qTOF-MS as a read-out for metabolite production.

We selected nine representative bacterial strains across numerous genera, including Gram-positive (Streptomyces, Amycolatopsis, and Bacillus) and Gram-negative bacteria (Burkholderia, Xenorhabdus, Phaeobacter, and Serratia). Most strains have previously been heavily mined for secondary metabolites; these were chosen to provide a rigorous test for the antibiotics hormesis approach. We conducted growth inhibition assays for each strain, wherein end point growth was plotted relative to a vehicle-treated control at high doses of the antibiotic library (Fig. 2). With Gram-negatives, Bacillus, and Amycolatopsis, we used optical density at 600 nm (OD600) to monitor growth, whereas the resazurin assay was used as a read-out with streptomycetes. Hits were defined as those antibiotics that reduced growth to 40% or less relative to the vehicle control. The screen identified 400 hits across the nine strains. These are tabulated for each strain along with the percent growth observed (SI Appendix, Table S2). For example, minocycline, spiramycin, and cefditoren were efficient high-dose killers with the actinomycetes, whereas thiamphenicol, rifabutin, and rifampicin appeared frequently with the Gram-negatives.

*Fig. 2.: Screening for high-dose growth-inhibitors. Viability of the nine bacterial strains indicated was determined after exposure to an FDA-approved antibiotic library at 20 μM final concentration. Absorbance at 600 nm (OD600, A–G) or the resazurin assay (H and I) were used to quantify growth. The threshold of viability (indicated by dotted line) is set at 40% growth relative to the vehicle control. Each circle represents the average of two independent measurements and reports on the effect of a single antibiotic from the library. Antibiotics that inhibited growth are shown in orange (SI Appendix, Table S2).*

To prioritize these, we selected 10 antibiotics per strain that exhibited the highest levels of growth inhibition and screened them against the corresponding strain at low-doses in the 1 to 5 μM range. Of the 90 antibiotics tested in this manner across nine diverse strains, we found 43% of high-dose growth inhibitors to induce a metabolic response at low doses, as determined by UPLC-qTOF-MS (Fig. 3). Overall, we noted distinct differential profiles with these antibiotics and recorded nearly a dozen previously unidentified metabolites per strain, highlighting the efficiency of this approach for triggering production of cryptic metabolites (SI Appendix, Figs. S1 and S2). We were able to rapidly dereplicate several known cryptic metabolites using the Dictionary of Natural Products (CHEMnetBASE); most of these are new to the strains we examined but previously characterized from other bacteria. For example, Amycolatopsis decaplanensis produced significant levels of octacosamicin A in response to low-dose minocycline (Fig. 3A and SI Appendix, Fig. S1) (25). Xenorhabdus beddingii was found to synthesize rhabdopeptide K in response to thiamphenicol (Fig. 3B) (26). Streptomyces canus produced octalactin B and canucin A in response to cefditoren and spiramycin, respectively (Fig. 3 C and D) (27, 28). Streptomyces parvus overproduced actinomycin D in the presence of low-dose methacycline (Fig. 3E) (29). Finally, we found prodigiosin and serramatolides in response to rifabutin in cultures of Serratia marcescens (Fig. 3 F–I) (30, 31). BGCs for each of these could be identified as well. More importantly, we identified several novel metabolites from Burkholderia pyrrocinia, X. beddingii, S. canus, and A. decaplanensis, and these compounds were next investigated further (Fig. 4 and SI Appendix, Fig. S2).

*Fig. 3.: Screening for low-dose elicitors of cryptic natural products. Extracted ion chromatograms of previously characterized, but cryptic metabolites: new-to-strain octacosamicin A from A. decaplanensis (A), new-to-strain rhabdopeptide A from X. beddingii (B), octalactin B and canucin A from S. canus (C and D), actinomycin D from S. parvus (E), and prodigiosin as well as serramatolides A and B from S. marcescens (F–H). The structures of the cryptic metabolites are shown (I).*

*Fig. 4.: Screening for low-dose elicitors of new cryptic natural products. Extracted ion chromatograms for new cryptic metabolites: pyrrocinamides from B. pyrrocinia in response to low-dose rifampicin (A–C), beddingiolide and xenoptides A/B from X. beddingii in the presence of low doses of trimethoprim and thiamphenicol, respectively (D–F), aspartocins F and G from S. canus in the presence of low-dose spiramycin (G and H), and octacosamicin C from A. decaplanensis in the presence of low-dose linezolid (I). (J) Structures of new analogs of previously known metabolites.*

Low-dose rifampicin triggers production of cryptic metabolites in B. pyrrocinia. Rifampicin was lethal to B. pyrrocinia at 20 μM. Low-dose rifampicin (1 μM), however, triggered production of several cryptic metabolites in a dose-dependent manner (Fig. 4 A–C). We purified three compounds from large-scale cultures in the presence of low-dose rifampicin and solved their structures using one-dimensional (1D)/two-dimensional (2D) NMR spectral analysis as well as high-resolution mass spectrometry (HR-MS). The most abundant of these, which we named pyrrocinamide A, purified as an amorphous solid with a deduced molecular formula of C20H42N2O2 and one degree of unsaturation (SI Appendix, Table S3). We observed one sp3 methyl group (δH 0.85; δC 14.4), 17 sp3 methylenes (δH 1.20 to 3.04; δC 22.6 to 37.4), one oxygenated methine group (δH 3.57; δC 68.0), and one amide-proton (δH 7.86) as a part of two spin systems (SI Appendix, Fig. S3 and Table S4). One of these consisted of an N-acylated 3-hydroxycadaverine substructure and the other of a straight-chain C16 acyl group. Two key HMBC correlations from the 1′-NH (7.86 ppm) and the C-2-H2 (35.8 ppm) to the C-1-carbonyl carbon (δC 172.8) indicated that the two spin systems are connected by an amide bond, thus accounting for the degree of unsaturation in pyrrocinamide A and completing its planar structure (Fig. 5A). Assignment of absolute configuration at C-2′ was first attempted with the phenylglycine methyl ester (PGME) method. However, the derivatized products were undetectable via HPLC–MS. As a result, we resorted to electronic circular dichroism (ECD) calculations (32). The experimental ECD spectrum of pyrrocinamide A showed a negative cotton effect at −220 nm (Fig. 5B). The calculated spectrum of the 2′- S diastereomer was close to the experimental ECD spectrum, indicating that C-2′ is S-configured.

*Fig. 5.: Structure elucidation of pyrrocinamides A–C from B. pyrrocinia. (A) Key NMR correlations used to solve the structures of pyrrocinamides A–C. (B) Configurational assignment at C-2′ of pyrrocinamide A using experimental ECD spectra and comparison to calculated ECD spectra for both R and S enantiomers. (C) Structures of pyrrocinamides A–C. Variants B and C are also shown as S-configured at C-2′, given the shared biosynthetic origin with pyrrocinamide A.*

Two additional compounds, pyrrocinamides B and C, were characterized with similar features (Fig. 5C). Both contained the N-acylated 3-hydroxycadaverine substructure but incorporated an olefin in the C16 (variant B) or C18 (variant C) acyl group, as evidenced by overlapping methine carbons (δC 130.2, SI Appendix, Figs. S4 and S5 and Tables S5 and S6). The position and geometry of the double bonds was marred by overlapping proton signals (δH ~5.34). To assign this feature, olefin cross-metathesis and subsequent HPLC–MS analysis were applied, ultimately demonstrating that it resides between C-11 and C-12 (Materials and Methods and SI Appendix, Fig. S6) (33). The configurations of the double bonds were established using 13C chemical shifts. It has been reported that aliphatic carbons adjacent to a Z-olefins in a long hydrocarbon chain resonate at δC 28 to 30 ppm, while those near an E-double bond resonate at δC 42 to 43 ppm allowing for a clear distinction between E/Z configurations (34). Since the chemical shifts of C-10 and C-13 were observed at δC 27.1 in pyrrocinamide B and δC 28.3 in pyrrocinamide C, the double bond in both variants was deduced to be Z-configured, thus completing the structure of the pyrrocinamides, new cryptic metabolites elicited using antibiotics hormesis (Fig. 5C).

Low-dose trimethoprim and beddingiolide production in X. beddingii. We likewise followed up on another cryptic metabolite elicited by low-dose trimethoprim in X. beddingii. Trimethoprim has been observed as a low-dose elicitor before and its mechanism of action has been addressed in Burkholderia thailandensis, where it triggered production of the cytotoxin malleicyprol/malleilactone (14). In X. beddingii, low-dose trimethoprim triggered production of a compound with a molecular formula, derived from HR-MS, of C24H42N2O6S with five degrees of unsaturation (Fig. 4D, SI Appendix, Table S3). This compound, which we termed beddingiolide, was not at all produced under standard growth conditions. Comprehensive analysis of 1D/2D NMR data revealed three carbonyl carbons (δC 173.1, 172.9, and 170.7), two olefinic carbons (δC 148.4 and 133.7), three oxygenated carbons (δC 80.0, 74.9, and 68.0), 12 aliphatic carbons (δC 39.1 to 24.5), one fully substituted carbon (δH 39.1), three methyl groups (δC 21.0, 20.3, and 14.0), two amide protons (δH 8.04 and 7.68), and two alcohols (δH 5.50 and 4.55) (Fig. 6A and SI Appendix, Fig. S7 and Table S7). Four out of the five degrees of unsaturation were explained by the existence of three carbonyl carbons and one double bond, suggesting that beddingiolide has a ring moiety.

*Fig. 6.: Structure elucidation of beddingiolide from X. beddingii. (A) Key NMR correlations used to solve the structure of beddingiolide. (B) Configurational assignment at C-4 and C-12 using experimental ECD spectra and comparison to calculated ECD spectra for the four diastereomers indicated. (C) Final structure of beddingiolide.*

Detailed analysis of a COSY NMR spectrum revealed six spin systems. Five of these were linked by HMBC correlations, revealing a pantetheine-like moiety, containing an alkylated thiol and an α, γ-dihydroxy-β, β-dimethyl acyl group. The other major spin system consisted of an octyl group. HMBC correlations, notably from H2–1′ (δH 2.18) and H-4 (δH 5.22), showed that these are linked through an α, β-unsaturated γ-lactone, thus establishing the planar structure of beddingiolide (Fig. 6A). In order to assign the absolute configurations of the two stereogenic centers, C-4 and C-12, ECD calculations were used. The CD spectrum of the isolated natural product matched the calculated (4R, 12R)-diastereomer, thus completing the structure of this unusual, substituted, and unsaturated γ-lactone (Fig. 6 B and C).

Xenoptides, cryptic cyclic depsipeptides induced by thiamphenicol. Beddingiolide was not the only cryptic metabolite produced by X. beddingii. Aside from trimethoprim, thiamphenicol also exhibited a high-dose killing and low-dose stimulating phenotype. Specifically, we observed induction of two large compounds with [M+H]+ of 1401.8738 and 1399.8618, molecules that had no matches in natural product databases and which we have termed xenoptides A and B, respectively. Isolation from large-scale cultures in the presence of thiamphenicol and extensive NMR and chemical analysis allowed us to solve the structures of these new peptides (SI Appendix, Figs. S8–S10). Comprehensive analysis of 1D/2D NMR data revealed the presence of two prolines, two threonines, four valines, two isoleucines, and one each of leucine, alanine, glycine, and the noncanonical amino acid, β-alanine. COSY/TOCSY correlations between H3–4′ (δH 0.86), H2–3′ (δH 1.46), and H2-2′ (δH 2.26 and 2.21), along with the HMBC correlations from H2-2′ to C-1′ (δC 171.7) assigned a butanoic acid moiety (N-Bu) (SI Appendix, Fig. S8 and Table S8). The 15 identified carbonyl groups and two prolines accounted for 17 out of 18 degrees of unsaturation, suggesting xenoptide A is a cyclic peptide. ROESY correlations between H2-2′ and H2-5 (δH 3.50 and 3.38) confirmed that the N-Bu moiety is linked at the N-terminus at Pro-1. Due to the presence of multiple aliphatic amino acids, such as Gly, Ala, Ile, Leu, and Val, the connectivity between amino acids was challenging to establish through HMBC and ROESY NMR spectral data alone, except for the linkages of N-Bu-Pro–Thr–Gly–Val–Val and Ala–β-Ala–Pro.

We resorted to detailed HR-MS/MS analysis of both the intact peptide and the base-catalyzed hydrolysate product, revealing the sequences of N-Bu-Pro–Thr–Gly–Val–Val–Ile/Leu and N-Bu-Pro–Thr–Gly–Val–Val–Ile/Leu–Thr–Val–Ile/Leu– Ile/Leu–Ala–β-Ala–Pro–Val, thus suggesting an ester linkage between Thr-2 and Val-4 (SI Appendix, Tables S9 and S10 and Figs. S11 and S12). We supplemented the data with xenoptide isolated in the presence of Ile-d10 or Leu-d10 to clarify the identities of these residues (SI Appendix, Figs. S13 and S14). We found Ile incorporation into the linear portion of the intact peptide and both Ile and Leu insertion into the hydrolysate, which ultimately led to the proposed structure shown for xenoptide A (Fig. 7).

*Fig. 7.: Structure elucidation and biosynthesis of xenoptides A and B. Shown is the xenoptide BGC, a proposed biosynthetic scheme, and the final structures of xenoptides A and B.*

Xenoptide B, a second analog, was analyzed in a similar manner, with the 1D NMR spectrum exhibiting a high similarity to that of variant A (SI Appendix, Fig. S9 and Table S11). Comprehensive analysis of its spectral properties showed that xenoptide B carries an additional double bond conjugated to a carbonyl group in the N-terminal acyl group, allowing us to identify it as trans-crotonic acid, thus completing the planar structures of the new cryptic cyclic depsipeptides (Fig. 7).

Advanced Marfey’s analysis showed the presence of both d/l-Thr and d/l -Val. To assign the absolute configurations of α-carbons in xenoptides, we sought to identify the xenoptide BGC. Initially, we analyzed the draft genome sequence of X. beddingii DSM 4764 using antiSMASH (version 7.0) (35). However, we could not locate a nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) BGC that contained 14 modules. The draft genome consisted of a number of contigs, suggesting that perhaps the whole BGC sequence had not been captured. We, therefore, resequenced the genome of X. beddingii DSM 4764 yielding a 3.87 Mb chromosome that revealed a large NRPS operon along with 14 other natural product BGCs, demonstrating a significant potential for secondary metabolite biosynthesis (SI Appendix, Table S12). The large NRPS BGC (SI Appendix, Table S13), ~65 kb in size, consists of three modular NRPSs (xnp C–E) that encode 14 modules with adenylation (A)-domain specificities (36) that matched the sequence inferred from HR-MS/ MS analysis: Pro-1–Thr-1–Gly–Val-1–Val-2–Ile-1–Thr-2–Val-3– Ile-2–Leu–Ala–β-Ala–Pro-2–Val-4. The A-domain specific to β-Ala was confirmed by manual inspection of the selectivity-conferring residues and comparison with the xenoamicins (37), a structurally related cyclic depsipeptide that also carries β-Ala (SI Appendix, Fig. S14). Further analysis suggested the presence of dual condensation/epimerization (C/E) domains in modules 3, 6, 8, 10, and 12, thus indicating that Thr-1, Val-2, Thr-2, Ile-2, and Ala are all d-configured (SI Appendix, Fig. S15) (38). These findings complete the structural assignment of the xenoptides and suggest a plausible biosynthetic pathway (Fig. 7).

Biological evaluation of novel cryptic metabolites. We explored any antimicrobial and antifungal activities of pyrrocinamides, beddingiolide, and xenoptides by conducting dose–response assays with Escherichia coli K12, Pseudomonas aeruginosa PAO1, S. marcescens NRRL B-2544, Bacillus subtilis 168, Enterococcus faecalis OG1RF, and Saccharomyces cerevisiae Y00000 (SI Appendix, Tables S14–S16). However, no inhibitory activity was observed against these strains under our assay conditions. The functions of these molecules remain to be determined; their production and isolation facilitate these future functional studies.

Additional cryptic metabolites. Finally, we identified several analogs of previously known natural products, which were characterized by HR-MS/MS-based dereplication and NMR spectroscopy (Fig. 4 G–J). We identified aspartocins F and G, two new analogs of a previously known class of acylated cyclic peptides with several non-canonical residues. These were induced by low-dose spiramycin in S. canus. We also identified octacosamicin C, a variant of the known compound from A. decaplanensis. This long, linear polyketide was identified from A. decaplanensis in response to low-dose minocycline (Fig. 4 I and J), adding three additional compounds to the group of nine new metabolites identified via antibiotic hormesis. These results also provide additional elicitor/cryptic metabolite pairs, which will enable detailed elicitor structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies in the future and allow us to examine why certain classes of antibiotics give rise to specific cryptic metabolites.

## Conclusions

Our prior studies showed that low-dose antibiotics are the most effective elicitors across numerous bacterial genera (7, 12–17). With several antibiotics, we examined the mechanism of induction and found them to act through the same target at low and high doses and use canonical stress response-related transcriptional regulators (13, 14). These observations set up a simple hypothesis that we have tested in the current study: High-dose growth-inhibitors can act as low-dose inducers of secondary metabolism. If true, it would provide for a remarkably simple approach for activating cryptic natural products with routine methods that have now been used for decades. This approach would consist of finding high-dose growth inhibitors using simple bioassays and screening these at low, subinhibitory doses to monitor cryptic metabolite production using facile read-outs, such as HPLC-MS. It would obviate any need for screening random culture variations such as in OSMAC (39), extensive cloning of gene clusters often conducted in heterologous expression or synthetic biology approaches, bacterial genetics in forward and reverse genetics approaches, or high-throughput small molecule screens in forward chemical genetics approaches (9).

Our results show that this antibiotic hormesis approach is highly effective and that screening a small number of high-dose growth inhibitors can yield low-dose elicitors. While we screened a library of 133 antibiotics, our results show that statistically a much smaller number will be sufficient: given that 43% of high-dose growth inhibitors acted as low-dose elicitors, the number of antibiotics can be significantly reduced to simplify the approach even further. The antibiotic hormesis method is thus the simplest yet among a cadre of approaches that have been developed in recent years to access natural products from sparingly expressed or transcriptionally silent BGCs.

The concentration-dependent effects of antibiotics have been known for some time, with low doses often eliciting profound, nonlethal physiological responses (4, 12, 40–44). Sublethal concentrations can trigger global transcriptional reprogramming, modulate quorum sensing, and alter biofilm dynamics. The ability of low-dose antibiotics to activate otherwise silent BGCs has emerged as a compelling extension of this concept and aside from using them to access cryptic metabolites, as we show in the current work, the insights into the low-dose regime suggest that antibiotics can function as cues that, through alteration of bacterial secondary metabolism, can reshape polymicrobial communities and microbiomes in diverse settings.

Future directions for this work are at least threefold. First, the biological activities of the newly identified cryptic metabolites remain to be fully established. In our initial antimicrobial and antifungal assays against the selected panel of strains, no inhibitory activities were observed under the conditions tested. Nevertheless, given their structural novelty, it is plausible that these molecules could exhibit interesting bioactivities. As many secondary metabolites are produced in response to competitive pressures in natural environments, their biological targets may span beyond bacteria, potentially including other eukaryotic strains or symbiotic hosts. Second, a key unanswered question is how sublethal antibiotics trigger the activation of silent BGCs. We have explored this question with trimethoprim and piperacillin (13, 14), but it needs to be examined more broadly and comprehensively to perhaps identify key governing principles or commonalities in this process. One intriguing hypothesis, borne out of studies with lethal doses, is that oxidative stress could be a common factor (13). We have observed oxidative stress with several antibiotics, including piperacillin, cephalosporins, and phenylpropanoids, but it remains to be seen if it underpins induction by low-dose antibiotics more broadly (13, 45). Understanding the molecular basis of this elicitation, including any underlying elicitor SAR, will be crucial for gaining fundamental insights into the ecological roles of secondary metabolites and the triggers that govern their production. Finally, the antibiotic hormesis approach can now be used systematically with any culturable microbial host in the search for yet new, cryptic natural products.

## Materials and Methods

Detailed descriptions of materials and methods, including generating the library of FDA-approved antibiotics; conducting high-dose growth inhibition assays using the antibiotic library with all nine strains; low-dose elicitation screens using UPLC-qTOF-MS with the selected strains; antimicrobial assays against selected strains; isolation of pyrrocinamides from B. pyrrocinia as well as beddingiolide and xenoptides from X. beddingii; structure elucidation of novel metabolites, including all 1D/2D NMR and HR–MS data; sequencing the genome of X. beddingii and identification of the xenoptide gene cluster; and discovery of the aspartocin and octacosamicin analogs are all given in SI Appendix.

## Supplementary Material

Microbial natural products are a rich source of therapeutic agents, yet many remain undiscovered due to the transcriptionally silent nature of their biosynthetic genes under standard laboratory conditions. Here, we present a simple and effective method to unlock this cryptic metabolome using a basic screening approach that relies on antibiotic hormesis, wherein high-dose growth-inhibitors are leveraged as low-dose stimulators of secondary metabolism. This is the simplest method yet for identifying cryptic metabolites as it avoids genetic procedures, molecular biology, or high-throughput screens. By facilitating access to previously hidden metabolites, this strategy opens avenues for natural product discovery and therapeutic lead identification. Beyond its practical utility, our findings motivate investigations into the mechanisms by which low-dose antibiotics affect microbial metabolism.
